`werk link` and `werk unlink` add or remove one typed link between two cards
why: Linking is the only way to write an edge, so every rule about which links are allowed is checked here, at the moment the link is made.

```
werk link <from> <to> --type refines|depends_on|supported_by|alternative_to [--why "..."]
werk unlink <from> <to> --type <t>
```

- A depends_on link needs `--why`: what <from> takes from <to> (#vi-prop-linkwhy). Without it, the command fails.
- Linking an existing depends_on pair again replaces its reason.
- A depends_on link to an ancestor or a descendant of <from> fails, and the message says why (#vi-prop-nolineage).
- A link on a ghost card is held until the card is accepted (#werk-propose-new).
- `werk unlink` removes one link from the map. The log keeps it.

card al-diff-cli-cover  [decided]
An op list that leaves a block unnamed is refused, not applied
why: applyOps rebuilds the body from the ops alone, so a block named in no op disappears on accept, with nothing in the diff to show it.

Every block of the current body must appear as the `old` of an `elaborated` or `removed` op. Keeping a block unchanged is `{"tag":"elaborated","old":X,"new":X}`. Dropping it on purpose is `{"tag":"removed","old":X}`, which the diff strikes through and the reader sees.

`propose` fails otherwise, and prints the blocks that were at risk. A deletion nobody can see and a deletion in the diff must not be the same call.

This is the same rule as the one al-diff-cli already applies to a quoted `old`: a claim the body does not support is never trusted silently. That rule checked the quotes that were given. This one checks the blocks that were not.

3	TITLE: Logic in a program. Markdown holds prompts only.
4	WHY: A skill is a prompt file. It cannot become a product.
5	BODY:
6	A pipeline has steps and rules. "Run the checks." "If they fail, try again up to five times." "A ticket moves to Done only with a linked pull request." Each rule lives in one of two places: in a skill file that an agent reads, or in a program that runs it.
7	
8	This card puts the rules in a program, a small TypeScript CLI. The state machine of the records, the checks on each state change, the tracker adapter, the rubric runner, and the loop controller live there. A skill file is a thin wrapper. It names the command to run and holds no rule of its own.
9	
10	## The two places
11	
12	| | Skill files (#pr-logic:opt0) | A program (this card) |
13	|---|---|---|
14	| Where a rule lives | Markdown text the agent reads | Code in the CLI |
15	| Who runs a loop | The agent reads "retry five times" and does it | The program counts to five |
16	| What the agent does | Every step | Only the steps that need judgement |
17	| An agent forgets a rule | Nothing stops it | The program refuses the action |
18	| Cost of a change | Edit a sentence | Edit code and its tests |
19	| Runs outside one agent harness | No | Yes |

21	## The boundary
22	
23	A step goes in the program if the same input must always give the same result. Examples: a state change, a staleness walk, a contract check, a retry cap, a time limit, a merge.
24	
25	A step goes in a prompt if it needs judgement. Examples: writing a spec, grading against a rubric, reviewing a diff, classifying a stuck agent.
26	
27	The program calls the prompt and parses the answer. The prompt returns an answer. The program decides what happens next.

=== #werk-remove [card decided]
TITLE: A card can be removed, not only rewritten
WHY: A map with a few wrong cards is not a broken map. Cleaning up one card must not mean rewriting it into something else.
BODY:
Removal is reversible and additive. A removed card leaves the map and nothing leaves the log. A person can restore it, and can list what is out. The verbs are listed in #werk-cli.

A removed card is gone from the tree, not struck through in place. Struck-through text keeps the noise it was meant to clear.

An agent never removes a card directly. It proposes the removal and the card shows it pending, like any other change.

Children: removal takes the refines subtree with it. A reparent option keeps the children and attaches them to the grandparent instead, for a bad parent over good children.

A removed card is out of every view and every edge touching it is out too. It makes nothing stale, counts in no rollup, and cites nothing. Restoring it returns the card and its edges as they were.

Removal takes the options and the excerpts of what it removes, not only the refines subtree. An option node sits nowhere in the tree, so one left behind is an orphan no view can reach and no later cleanup can find. A source two cards cite stays while either of them stays.

The control and its confirmation are drawn in the card view: see #vi-remove-btn.

=== #werk-wording [card decided]
TITLE: A card's words describe its own subject, not the session that wrote it
WHY: A card is read later, cold, by someone who needs to act on its subject. Session facts (who said what, what came before, what stage the conversation was at) are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight.
BODY:
No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour, concepts, and the commands and flags a person types. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.
